title: French Fry-Sized Fish Climbs a 50-Foot Waterfall!
summary: Have you ever tried to climb a slippery rock wall with water rushing down on you? It sounds impossible, right? Well, there's a tiny fish in Africa that does exactly that! In the Democratic Republic of Congo, shellear fish climb the steep 50-foot Luvilombo Falls. These fish are no bigger than a French fry, but they can scale a wall of rock against the force of rushing water. Scientists finally proved this in a new study. P. Kiwele Mutambala, a Ph.D. student, watched the fish in 2018 and 2020. He said, 'It's as if the fish is swimming but in vertical. It's beyond imagination.' So how do they do it? The fish's front fins are covered with microscopic hooks that grip the rock like Velcro. Their back fins help push them upward. But it's still a super tough job. The fish inch up the edges to avoid the strongest currents. They move in short bursts and often stop to rest for up to an hour at a time. Many slip and tumble back down, so they have to start over. One climb can take as long as 10 hours! Only young fish under two inches try this. Older, bigger fish are too heavy. Scientists aren't sure why they climb. Maybe they're looking for better food, safer homes, or mates. These shellears are the first climbing fish found in Africa, but they're not the only ones. In Hawaii, stream gobies climb waterfalls too, using a suction cup on their bellies. Nature is full of amazing surprises!
why_it_matters: This story shows that even the smallest creatures can accomplish amazing things, reminding us to never give up even when a task seems impossible.
